abstract: Humans are excellent at recognizing materials like food, soil or paper, which is crucial for many everyday tasks. We generally enjoy vivid intuitions about what surfaces would feel like, without reaching out and touching them. While this capability is understandable for familiar materials, how does the brain interpret stuff we have never encountered before? We hypothesized that the need to distinguish useful or hazardous substances by sight led to the ability to infer material properties from the very first encounter. To test this, we used generative AI to synthesize realistic images of new 'hybrid' materials, by fusing characteristics of images from different 'parent' categories (e.g., bark x carpet). Even though the hybrid materials have never existed in the real world--and observers judged them to be far less familiar than their parents--we found that they elicited a rich and compelling phenomenology, and yielded consistent inferences about their likely physical and multisensory properties, such as what they would feel like to touch. Their perceived properties occupied the same broad multidimensional space as familiar materials, whereas phase-scrambled controls did not. Our findings suggest that the visual system exploits generalizable relationships between visual appearance and physical properties, enabling instantaneous interpretation of new kinds of 'stuff'.
